claims.claim: Hannah Arendt is characterized as the theorist of beginnings whose work, particularly The Human Condition, is highly original and idiosyncratic.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Hannah Arendt is preeminently the theorist of beginnings. All her books are tales of the unexpected (whether concerned with the novel horrors of totalitarianism or the new dawn of revolution), and reflections on the human capacity to start something new pervade her thinking.

claims.claim: Arendt explicitly denied that she intended to propose a blueprint for the future or write political philosophy as conventionally understood.
qualifications: Repudiating the title of political philosopher
claims.supporting_excerpt: But she emphatically denied that her role as a political thinker was to propose a blueprint for the future or to tell anyone what to do. Repudiating the title of “political philosopher,” she argued that the mistake made by all political philosophers since Plato has been to ignore the fundamental condition of politics

must_not_be_lost: The Human Condition is crammed with distinctions such as labor, work, and action.
Arendt uses ancient Greece as an Archimedean point to criticize modern thinking.
extraction.segment_function: Introduction to Hannah Arendt's work and The Human Condition, highlighting her focus on beginnings, characteristic use of distinctions, critical reliance on ancient Greece, and rejection of traditional political philosophy or utopian prescriptions.

claims.claim: The immediate reaction to the launch of the man-made satellite was not triumphal pride, but relief regarding the first step toward escaping human imprisonment to the earth.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The immediate reaction, expressed on the spur of the moment, was relief about the first “step toward escape from men’s imprisonment to the earth.”

claims.claim: The question of whether to use new scientific and technical knowledge to exchange given human existence for something self-made is a political question of the first order rather than a purely scientific one.
qualifications: cannot be decided by scientific means
can hardly be left to the decision of professional scientists or professional politicians alone
claims.supporting_excerpt: The question is only whether we wish to use our new scientific and technical knowledge in this direction, and this question cannot be decided by scientific means; it is a political question of the first order and therefore can hardly be left to the decision of professional scientists or professional politicians.

definitions.definition: The very quintessence of the human condition and a unique habitat providing humans with a place to move and breathe without effort and without artifice.

distinctions.distinction: The human artifice separates human existence from mere animal environments, whereas life itself remains outside this artificial world, through which man stays related to all other living organisms.

must_not_be_lost: The characterization of the earth as the quintessence of the human condition.
The rebellion against given human existence through scientific and technical power.
extraction.segment_function: The prologue introduces the 1957 launch of the earth-satellite, interpreting it as an expression of a deep-seated human desire to escape the earth and the human condition, and framing contemporary scientific ambitions to artificially alter human life and biology as political questions of the highest order.
unresolved_context: Discussion of science fiction as a vehicle of mass sentiments and mass desires.
Specific scientific attempts involving test-tube life, frozen germ plasm, and extended life-spans.

claims.claim: The term vita activa designates three fundamental human activities: labor, work, and action.
claims.supporting_excerpt: With the term vita activa , I propose to designate three fundamental human activities: labor, work, and action.

claims.claim: Action corresponds to the human condition of plurality and is specifically the condition of all political life.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Action, the only activity that goes on directly between men without the intermediary of things or matter, corresponds to the human condition of plurality, to the fact that men, not Man, live on the earth and inhabit the world. While all aspects of the human condition are somehow related to politics, this plurality is specifically the condition—not only the conditio sine qua non , but the conditio per quam —of all political life.

definitions.definition: The activity corresponding to the biological process of the human body, bound to vital necessities, whose human condition is life itself.
The activity corresponding to the unnaturalness of human existence that provides an artificial world of things meant to outlast and transcend individuals, with the condition of worldliness.
The only activity that goes on directly between men without the intermediary of things or matter, corresponding to human plurality.

distinctions.distinction: Labor corresponds to the biological process and vital necessities of the human body, whereas work corresponds to the unnaturalness of human existence and provides an artificial world of things distinct from natural surroundings.

must_not_be_lost: The connection of all three activities to birth and death, natality and mortality.
The conceptualization of men as conditioned beings.
extraction.segment_function: Define the vita activa, its three fundamental activities (labor, work, action), their corresponding human conditions, and their relationship to natality, mortality, and general human conditioning.

claims.claim: Action is the exclusive prerogative of man and is entirely dependent upon the constant presence of others, whereas labor and work do not strictly require the company of others in the same way.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Action alone is the exclusive prerogative of man; neither a beast nor a god is capable of it, 1 and only action is entirely dependent upon the constant presence of others.

claims.claim: The translation of Aristotle's zōon politikon as animal socialis or homo est naturaliter politicus, id est, socialis reflects a loss of the original Greek understanding of politics.
claims.supporting_excerpt: More than any elaborate theory, this unconscious substitution of the social for the political betrays the extent to which the original Greek understanding of politics had been lost.

definitions.definition: Human life in so far as it is actively engaged in doing something, always rooted in a world of men and of man-made things.

distinctions.distinction: A citizen's second life in the city-state belonging to the communal order, distinct from what is one's own.

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between action, labor, and work regarding the presence of others.
Historical transition from zōon politikon to animal socialis.
extraction.segment_function: The author introduces Chapter II on the public and private realm, examining the concepts of the political versus the social animal, the human condition of living together, and the classical Greek distinction between the polis and the household.

claims.claim: The Greek political consciousness clearly and articulately distinguished activities sustaining the life process from the political realm, barring them from entry.
claims.supporting_excerpt: At the root of Greek political consciousness we find an unequaled clarity and articulateness in drawing this distinction. No activity that served only the purpose of making a living, of sustaining only the life process, was permitted to enter the political realm

claims.claim: The emergence of society from the household into the public sphere blurred the boundary between private and political and altered the meaning of both terms.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The emergence of society—the rise of housekeeping, its activities, problems, and organizational devices—from the shadowy interior of the household into the light of the public sphere, has not only blurred the old borderline between private and political, it has also changed almost beyond recognition the meaning of the two terms and their significance for the life of the individual and the citizen.

distinctions.distinction: In ancient feeling, privacy had a privative trait meaning deprivation of the highest capacities, whereas modern privacy is associated with an enormous enrichment through individualism and serves to shelter the intimate against the social realm.

extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: The law of the ancient city-state was originally identified with the spatial boundary or no man's land between the household and the public realm, serving as a wall that both separated and protected them.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The law originally was identified with this boundary line, 62 which in ancient times was still actually a space, a kind of no man’s land 63 between the private and the public, sheltering and protecting both realms while, at the same time, separating them from each other.

claims.claim: Private wealth became a condition for admission to public life because it assured that its owner was free from the necessity of providing for his own livelihood and could participate in public activity.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Private wealth, therefore, became a condition for admission to public life not because its owner was engaged in accumulating it but, on the contrary, because it assured with reasonable certainty that its owner would not have to engage in providing for himself the means of use and consumption and was free for public activity.

definitions.definition: A wall-like, sacred boundary separating and protecting the private household from the public political community.

distinctions.distinction: Privacy and property as a dark, hidden space ensuring freedom are of a different historical origin than the political significance of private wealth used to master the necessities of life.
distinctions.item_a: Property as a private place and condition for freedom
distinctions.item_b: Private wealth as a source of income and livelihood

must_not_be_lost: The ancient conception of law as a spatial wall separating the private household from the public realm.
The historical role of private wealth in securing freedom from necessity rather than in accumulating capital.
extraction.segment_function: Discussion of the historical and political significance of law, the boundary between the public and private realms, private property, and wealth in relation to freedom and the modern age.

claims.claim: The distinction between labor and work proposed by the author is unusual and lacks substantial precedent in either pre-modern political tradition or modern labor theories.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The distinction between labor and work which I propose is unusual. The phenomenal evidence in its favor is too striking to be ignored, and yet historically it is a fact that apart from a few scattered remarks, which moreover were never developed even in the theories of their authors, there is hardly anything in either the pre-modern tradition of political thought or in the large body of modern labor theories to support it.

claims.claim: Every European language, both ancient and modern, contains two etymologically unrelated words for what has come to be thought of as the same activity.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Against this scarcity of historical evidence, however, stands one very articulate and obstinate testimony, namely, the simple fact that every European language, ancient and modern, contains two etymologically unrelated words for what we have to come to think of as the same activity, and retains them in the face of their persistent synonymous usage.

definitions.definition: A later term for artisans whose chief interest is their craft and not the market place.

distinctions.distinction: Every European language contains two etymologically unrelated words for these activities, and the noun form of labor never designates a finished product while the product itself is invariably derived from the word for work.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between labor and work is etymologically preserved across European languages despite synonymous usage.
Contempt for laboring historically arose from a striving for freedom from necessity and effort that left no permanent monument.
extraction.segment_function: Introduction to the chapter on labor, addressing the author's departure from Marx, introducing the unusual distinction between labor and work grounded in etymological evidence across European languages, and explaining the historical contempt for laboring in ancient thought.
unresolved_context: Discussion of Karl Marx to follow in the chapter.
Specific etymological linguistic details regarding Locke, Greek terminology, and historical shifts in the polis.

claims.claim: Ancient ancients did not despise labor and work simply because slaves were engaged in them; rather, they felt it necessary to possess slaves because all occupations serving the maintenance of life had a slavish nature.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The opinion that labor and work were despised in antiquity because only slaves were engaged in them is a prejudice of modern historians. The ancients reasoned the other way around and felt it necessary to possess slaves because of the slavish nature of all occupations that served the needs for the maintenance of life.

claims.claim: The institution of slavery in antiquity functioned as an attempt to exclude labor from the conditions of man's life rather than as a device for cheap labor or profit-driven exploitation.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The institution of slavery in antiquity, though not in later times, was not a device for cheap labor or an instrument of exploitation for profit but rather the attempt to exclude labor from the conditions of man’s life.

must_not_be_lost: The enslavement to necessity in ancient thought and its relation to slavery and the vita activa.
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: Both Smith and Marx shared a contempt for unproductive labor and menial servants who leave nothing behind in return for their consumption.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Moreover, both Smith and Marx were in agreement with modern public opinion when they despised unproductive labor as parasitical, actually a kind of perversion of labor, as though nothing were worthy of this name which did not enrich the world. Marx certainly shared Smith’s contempt for the “menial servants” who like “idle guests . . . leave nothing behind them in return for their consumption.”

claims.claim: Marx's introduction of the term labor power (Arbeitskraft) was considered by Engels to be the most original and revolutionary element of his entire system.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is because not labor itself but the surplus of human “labor power ” ( Arbeits kraft) explains labor’s productivity that Marx’s introduction of this term, as Engels rightly remarked, constituted the most original and revolutionary element of his whole system.

definitions.definition: A human power whose strength is not exhausted by producing the means of its own subsistence and survival, but is capable of producing a surplus beyond what is necessary for its own reproduction.

distinctions.distinction: The productivity of work adds new objects to the human artifice, whereas the productivity of labor power produces objects only incidentally, is primarily concerned with the means of its own reproduction, and never produces anything but life.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between productive and unproductive labor conceals the more fundamental distinction between work and labor.
Under a completely socialized mankind focused entirely on the life process, the distinction between labor and work would completely disappear as all things become functions of the life process.
extraction.segment_function: Analyze the historical and theoretical conflation of productive labor, unproductive labor, work, and labor power in modern economic theory, particularly through the views of Smith and Marx.

claims.claim: The distinctions between skilled and unskilled labor and between intellectual and manual work play no role in classical political economy or in Marx's work.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is interesting to note that the distinctions between skilled and unskilled and between intellectual and manual work play no role in either classical political economy or in Marx’s work.

definitions.definition: What is bought and sold in the modern labor market as a result of the division of labor abolishing individual skill, of which each living human being possesses approximately the same amount.

distinctions.distinction: Unskilled work is a contradiction in terms, as every activity requires a certain amount of skill; the distinction notes only stages and qualities within activities rather than different activities.
Liberal arts involve prudent judgment and public relevance, whereas servile arts or trades are considered sordid and unbecoming for a full-fledged citizen.

extraction.segment_function: Examine the distinctions between skilled and unskilled labor and between manual and intellectual work, tracing their historical and modern significance.

claims.claim: The distinction between labor and work becomes merely a difference in degree if the worldly character, location, function, and length of stay of the produced thing are not taken into account.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It seems that the distinction between labor and work, which our theorists have so obstinately neglected and our languages so stubbornly preserved, indeed becomes merely a difference in degree if the worldly character of the produced thing—its location, function, and length of stay in the world—is not taken into account.

claims.claim: The products of work guarantee the permanence and durability without which a world would not be possible at all, whereas consumer goods are for incessant consumption and lack stability.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Viewed as part of the world, the products of work—and not the products of labor—guarantee the permanence and durability without which a world would not be possible at all.

definitions.definition: Things needed by our bodies and produced by laboring that have no stability of their own and appear and disappear for incessant consumption.
Things in an environment that are used rather than consumed, to which men become accustomed, and which give rise to the familiarity of the world, its customs, and habits.

distinctions.distinction: Consumer goods are for incessant consumption to assure life's survival and disappear, whereas use objects are items in an environment that are used rather than consumed and provide familiarity and stability.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between labor and work depends on the worldly character and permanence of the things produced.
Products of action, speech, and thought are unworldly and futile, depending on reification (materialization into tangible things like books, monuments, or art) to remain in the world.
extraction.segment_function: The author defines and distinguishes consumer goods, use objects, and the products of action and speech based on their worldly character, durability, and dependence on reification.

claims.claim: The least durable tangible things are those needed for the life process itself, which are consumed by use or perish quickly through decay.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The least durable of tangible things are those needed for the life process itself. Their consumption barely survives the act of their production; in the words of Locke, all those “good things” which are “really useful to the life of man,” to the “necessity of subsisting,” are “generally of short duration, such as—if they are not consumed by use—will decay and perish by themselves.”

claims.claim: Laboring always moves in a repetitive circle prescribed by the biological process of the living organism, having no proper beginning or end until the organism dies.
claims.supporting_excerpt: laboring always moves in the same circle, which is prescribed by the biological process of the living organism and the end of its “toil and trouble” comes only with the death of this organism.

definitions.definition: Human life as a linear time interval between birth and death, full of events that can be told as a story and establish a biography.
Mere biological life shared with other living things, retaining the cyclical movement of nature.

distinctions.distinction: Bios is human life as a linear interval between birth and death capable of forming a story or biography, whereas zōē is the mere biological life process shared with other living things that retains a cyclical movement.

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between perishable things needed for life and the durable human artifice.
The connection between labor and the cyclical movement of the biological life process.
extraction.segment_function: Explaining the characteristics of labor, the biological life process, and their relation to nature's cyclical movement versus the human world's permanence.

claims.claim: Marx defined labor physiologically as man's metabolism with nature, placing labor and consumption as two stages of the biological life cycle.
claims.supporting_excerpt: When Marx defined labor as “man’s metabolism with nature,” in whose process “nature’s material [is] adapted by a change of form to the wants of man,” so that “labour has incorporated itself with its subject,” he indicated clearly that he was “speaking physiologically” and that labor and consumption are but two stages of the ever-recurring cycle of biological life.

claims.claim: Locke, Smith, and Marx each held that labor was the supreme world-building capacity of man, which led them into genuine contradictions due to equating work with labor.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Of the three, however, only Marx was interested in labor as such; Locke was concerned with the institution of private property as the root of society and Smith wished to explain and to secure the unhampered progress of a limitless accumulation of wealth. But all three, though Marx with greatest force and consistency, held that labor was considered to be the supreme world-building capacity of man, and since labor actually is the most natural and least worldly of man’s activities, each of them, and again none more than Marx, found himself in the grip of certain genuine contradictions.

definitions.definition: An activity that follows the exigencies of the biological life process, functioning as a devouring process of consumption and metabolism with nature, as well as an unending fight against the decay of the world.

distinctions.distinction: Labor prepares matter for destruction and incorporation through consumption and fights natural decay, whereas work changes matter in order to work upon it and use the finished durable product without destroying it in a swift natural metabolism.

extraction.segment_function: To analyze labor as a biological metabolism with nature and a destructive, consuming process that is distinct from work, tracing its theoretical elevation through Locke, Smith, and Marx while highlighting the contradictions arising from the conflation of work with labor.

claims.claim: Locke had to introduce money as a lasting thing to allow the laboring body to become the origin of property, because labor naturally produces only things of short duration.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Thus Locke, in order to save labor from its manifest disgrace of producing only “things of short duration,” had to introduce money—a “lasting thing which men may keep without spoiling”—a kind of deus ex machina without which the laboring body, in its obedience to the life process, could never have become the origin of anything so permanent and lasting as property

claims.claim: Marx's thought contains a fundamental contradiction wherein he defines man as an animal laborans while maintaining that human emancipation requires liberation from labor rather than its glorification.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The fact remains that in all stages of his work he defines man as an animal laborans and then leads him into a society in which this greatest and most human power is no longer necessary. We are left with the rather distressing alternative between productive slavery and unproductive freedom.

definitions.definition: A term used by Marx to define man through labor as an eternal necessity imposed by nature.

distinctions.distinction: The proportion between what nature gives and what man adds is opposite in the products of labor and work; consumption goods never completely lose their naturalness (e.g., grain in bread), whereas work reifies and creates an objective world of things where the raw material disappears.

must_not_be_lost: Locke's reliance on money to bridge the gap between ephemeral labor and durable property
Marx's contradiction between labor as human essence and the political goal of emancipating man from labor
extraction.segment_function: Analyze the contradictions in Locke, Smith, and Marx regarding labor, distinguishing between labor and work, and highlighting Marx's foundational contradiction between glorifying labor and seeking emancipation from it.

claims.claim: Locke grounded private property in the body, treating labor as a world-appropriating activity rooted in the ultimate privacy of the human person.
qualifications: applies specifically to Locke's philosophical justification of appropriation
claims.supporting_excerpt: Locke founded private property on the most privately owned thing there is, “the property [of man] in his own person,” that is, in his own body.

claims.claim: Hedonism and the pursuit of an absent of pain represent the most radical forms of a non-political, totally private way of life centered on bodily sensations.
qualifications: linked to consistent sensualism and the historical tradition of Epicurean and Stoic withdrawal
claims.supporting_excerpt: Hedonism, the doctrine that only bodily sensations are real, is but the most radical form of a non-political, totally private way of life, the true fulfilment of Epicurus’ lathe biōsas kai mē politeuesthai (“live in hiding and do not care about the world”).

definitions.definition: The doctrine that only bodily sensations are real, serving as the most radical form of a non-political, totally private way of life.

distinctions.distinction: Locke's argument for the privacy of appropriation rests on bodily activity, which is distinguished from the very different argument for the privacy of property.

must_not_be_lost: Locke's derivation of private property from the body
The connection between bodily life, labor, and the modern growth of wealth
The characterization of hedonism and bodily pain as the basis for a totally private, non-political life
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: Pain and the experience of release from pain are uniquely independent from the world because they contain no experience of any worldly object.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In any event, pain and the concomitant experience of release from pain are the only sense experiences that are so independent from the world that they do not contain the experience of any worldly object.

claims.claim: Laboring is the only activity that corresponds strictly to worldlessness or the loss of world found in pain, as the body remains imprisoned in its metabolism with nature.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The only activity which corresponds strictly to the experience of worldlessness, or rather to the loss of world that occurs in pain, is laboring, where the human body, its activity notwithstanding, is also thrown back upon itself, concentrates upon nothing but its own being alive, and remains imprisoned in its metabolism with nature without ever transcending or freeing itself from the recurring cycle of its own functioning.

must_not_be_lost: Pain and tickling as extreme examples used by modern philosophy to doubt the senses.
Locke's concept of private property as an enclosure from the common that mitigates labor's unrelatedness to the world.
The shift toward infinite accumulation and the socialized mankind where individual life-spans and property limits are superseded by the species life process.
extraction.segment_function: Analyze the worldlessness of pain and labor, the nature of bodily sensation, and how private property and the modern process of wealth accumulation relate to the life process and world-alienation.

claims.claim: The concept of process, common to nineteenth-century sciences like economics, history, biology, and geology, was virtually unknown prior to the modern age and became modeled after the biological life process known through introspection, which corresponds to labor.
claims.supporting_excerpt: What all these theories in the various sciences—economics, history, biology, geology—have in common is the concept of process, which was virtually unknown prior to the modern age. Since the discovery of processes by the natural sciences had coincided with the discovery of introspection in philosophy, it is only natural that the biological process within ourselves should eventually become the very model of the new concept; within the framework of experiences given to introspection, we know of no other process but the life process within our bodies, and the only activity into which we can translate it and which corresponds to it is labor.

claims.claim: Neither abundance of goods nor shortened labor time can establish a common world, and an expropriated animal laborans remains private even when deprived of a protective private place, leading to worldless activities like hobbies under socialized conditions.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Neither abundance of goods nor the shortening of the time actually spent in laboring are likely to result in the establishment of a common world, and the expropriated animal laborans becomes no less private because he has been deprived of a private place of his own to hide and be protected from the common realm.

definitions.definition: Man conceptualized through labor, driven by bodily needs and maintenance, whose activity is oblivious to the world to the point of worldlessness.

distinctions.distinction: The animal laborans is driven by bodily needs and does not use its body freely, whereas homo faber uses his hands and primordial tools freely.

must_not_be_lost: The connection between the modern concept of process, biological life, and labor.
Marx's prediction of the withering away of the public realm and the rise of worldless hobbies for socialized men.
The inherent worldlessness of the animal laborans and mass society of laborers.
extraction.segment_function: Examines the historical emergence of the modern concept of process across sciences, its intimate link to the biological life process and labor, and the consequent privatization and worldlessness of a mass society of laborers.

claims.claim: The animal laborans is ejected from the world because of being imprisoned in the privacy of the body and caught in the fulfillment of unshareable and uncommunicable needs.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The animal laborans does not flee the world but is ejected from it in so far as he is imprisoned in the privacy of his own body, caught in the fulfilment of needs in which nobody can share and which nobody can fully communicate.

claims.claim: Pain and effort are the modes in which life and necessity make themselves felt, such that their complete elimination would deprive human life of its liveliness and vitality.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The human condition is such that pain and effort are not just symptoms which can be removed without changing life itself; they are rather the modes in which life itself, together with the necessity to which it is bound, makes itself felt.

definitions.definition: A condition characterized by worldlessness, imprisonment in bodily privacy, and the fulfillment of unshareable biological needs.

distinctions.distinction: The animal laborans does not flee the world voluntarily but is ejected from it by being imprisoned in bodily privacy and necessity.
distinctions.item_b: active flight from publicity inherent in good works

distinctions.distinction: Trust in world reality derives from the permanence and durability of the world, whereas trust in life reality depends on the intensity and impact with which life is felt.
distinctions.item_a: trust in the reality of the world
distinctions.item_b: trust in the reality of life

must_not_be_lost: The connection between ancient slavery, biological life burdens, and the ancient city-state as a consumption center.
The idea that pain and effort are constitutive of human vitality rather than mere removable symptoms.
extraction.segment_function: To analyze the biological burden of life, the role of ancient slavery, and the relationship between the necessity of pain and effort and human vitality versus worldliness.

claims.claim: Modern improvements in labor tools, such as mute robots, have made the effort of sustaining life and giving birth easier, but they have not eliminated compulsion or human subjection to necessity.
qualifications: has made labor easier and less painful
has not eliminated compulsion or the condition of being subject to need and necessity
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is true that the enormous improvement in our labor tools—the mute robots with which homo faber has come to the help of the animal laborans , as distinguished from the human, speaking instruments (the instrumentum vocale , as the slaves in ancient households were called) whom the man of action had to rule and oppress when he wanted to liberate the animal laborans from its bondage—has made the twofold labor of life, the effort of its sustenance and the pain of giving birth, easier and less painful than it has ever been. This, of course, has not eliminated compulsion from the laboring activity or the condition of being subject to need and necessity from human life.

claims.claim: Tools and instruments are products of work rather than labor, and while they can ease labor and multiply human strength, no work can be produced without tools.
qualifications: not a product of labor but of work
birth of homo faber and the coming into being of a man-made world of things are coeval with the discovery of tools and instruments
claims.supporting_excerpt: Tools and instruments which can ease the effort of labor considerably are themselves not a product of labor but of work; they do not belong in the process of consumption but are part and parcel of the world of use objects. Their role, no matter how great it may be in the labor of any given civilization, can never attain the fundamental importance of tools for all kinds of work. No work can be produced without tools, and the birth of homo faber and the coming into being of a man-made world of things are actually coeval with the discovery of tools and instruments.

definitions.definition: The human condition or aspect focused on the endless cycle of biological life and labor, requiring sustenance and service.
The maker or fabricator of the man-made world of things, whose activities result in tools, instruments, and use objects.
Living, speaking instruments, historically referring to slaves in ancient households who served the living process rather than producing durable works.

distinctions.distinction: Tools of workmanship result in something more than the mere use of the instrument and have a controllable end in a finished product, whereas household instruments are tied to the endless, consuming process of living.
distinctions.item_b: Instruments of the household / living service

must_not_be_lost: Freedom requires knowing that one is subject to necessity.
Household slaves in antiquity were instruments of living rather than instruments of making things or production.
The endless process of life requires a perpetuum mobile or a living organism to serve it, which inanimate tools and gadgets cannot fully replace.
extraction.segment_function: The author analyzes the distinction and relationship between labor tools and work instruments, contrasting modern robotic assistance with ancient slavery, and explaining why tools of production can never fully replace the living service required by the endless biological process of life.

claims.claim: Division of labor grows directly out of the laboring process and must be distinguished from the specialization of work.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Division of labor indeed grows directly out of the laboring process and should not be mistaken for the apparently similar principle of specialization which prevails in working processes and with which it is usually equated.

claims.claim: Specialization of work is guided by the finished product requiring different pooled skills, whereas division of labor presupposes qualitative equivalence and exchangeability of activities requiring no special skill.
claims.supporting_excerpt: specialization of work is essentially guided by the finished product itself, whose nature it is to require different skills which then are pooled and organized together, division of labor, on the contrary, presupposes the qualitative equivalence of all single activities for which no special skill is required

definitions.definition: A principle based on the qualitative equivalence of all single activities requiring no special skill, representing amounts of labor power added together in a purely quantitative way.
A principle prevailing in working processes that is guided by the finished product, requiring different skills which are pooled and organized together.

distinctions.distinction: Division of labor presupposes the qualitative equivalence of all single activities requiring no special skill and is based on a collective labor force, whereas specialization is guided by a finished product requiring different pooled skills.

must_not_be_lost: Division of labor and specialization share only a general principle of organization rooted in the political capacity to act together.
Mass production depends on replacing workmen and specialization with laborers and the division of labor.
extraction.segment_function: To analyze and distinguish the division of labor from the specialization of work, contrasting their underlying principles, outcomes, and roles in modern mass production.

claims.claim: The ideals of homo faber, emphasizing permanence and durability, have been sacrificed to the ideal of abundance championed by the animal laborans.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The ideals of homo faber , the fabricator of the world, which are permanence, stability, and durability, have been sacrificed to abundance, the ideal of the animal laborans.

claims.claim: A consumers' society arose not through the political emancipation of the laboring classes, but through the emancipation of the laboring activity itself.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This society did not come about through the emancipation of the laboring classes but by the emancipation of the laboring activity itself, which preceded by centuries the political emancipation of laborers.

definitions.definition: A society of laborers where labor and consumption are two stages of the same process, and human activities are leveled to the common denominator of securing the necessities of life and providing for their abundance.

distinctions.distinction: Homo faber is the fabricator of the world whose ideals are permanence, stability, and durability, whereas animal laborans is associated with the pursuit of abundance.

must_not_be_lost: The transition from a society valuing permanence and durability (homo faber) to a consumers' society valuing abundance (animal laborans).
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: All civilizations prior to the modern era viewed the art of earning money as separate from the actual content of other arts and aimed at keeping the worker free from the necessity to labor.
claims.supporting_excerpt: all civilizations prior to our own would rather have agreed with Plato that the “art of earning money” ( technē mistharnētikē ) is entirely unconnected with the actual content even of such arts as medicine, navigation, or architecture, which were attended by monetary rewards.

claims.claim: The modern age's emancipation of labor brought progress toward non-violence, but its status as progress toward freedom is much less certain.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The emancipation of labor and the concomitant emancipation of the laboring classes from oppression and exploitation certainly meant progress in the direction of non-violence. It is much less certain that it was also progress in the direction of freedom.

must_not_be_lost: Emancipation of labor vs freedom
Marx's view on emancipation from labor and necessity
Role of violence and necessity in antiquity versus the modern age
extraction.segment_function: Examines the distinction between the emancipation of labor and freedom, contrasting ancient views on necessity and violence with modern trends, automation, and Marx's concept of emancipation from labor.

claims.claim: The danger of future automation lies in human productivity being absorbed into an intensified life process that follows an automatic cycle, wearing down world durability.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The danger of future automation is less the much deplored mechanization and artificialization of natural life than that, its artificiality notwithstanding, all human productivity would be sucked into an enormously intensified life process and would follow automatically, without pain or effort, its ever-recurrent natural cycle.

claims.claim: The spare time of the animal laborans is spent entirely on consumption rather than higher activities, and increased free time only intensifies craving appetites.
claims.supporting_excerpt: the spare time of the animal laborans is never spent in anything but consumption, and the more time left to him, the greedier and more craving his appetites.

must_not_be_lost: The triumph over necessity achieved by the modern world through the emancipation of labor leads to mass culture and universal unhappiness because the animal laborans occupies the public realm.
extraction.segment_function: To analyze how a society dominated by the animal laborans and modern automation risks consuming the world, and how the triumph over necessity through the emancipation of labor results in mass culture and universal unhappiness.

claims.claim: The transformation of our economy into a waste economy, where goods are rapidly devoured and discarded, serves as an obvious danger sign indicating we are moving toward the ideal of the animal laborans.
claims.supporting_excerpt: One of the obvious danger signs that we may be on our way to bring into existence the ideal of the animal laborans is the extent to which our whole economy has become a waste economy, in which things must be almost as quickly devoured and discarded as they have appeared in the world, if the process itself is not to come to a sudden catastrophic end.

claims.claim: The human world is composed not of consumed items, but of things that are used, providing the condition under which human life can be at home on earth.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The world, the man-made home erected on earth and made of the material which earthly nature delivers into human hands, consists not of things that are consumed but of things that are used. If nature and the earth generally constitute the condition of human life , then the world and the things of the world constitute the condition under which this specifically human life can be at home on earth.

definitions.definition: An economy in which things must be almost as quickly devoured and discarded as they appear in the world to prevent a catastrophic end to the process.
The man-made home erected on earth consisting of things that are used rather than consumed, which constitutes the condition under which specifically human life can be at home.

distinctions.distinction: Things that are consumed belong to the domain of the animal laborans and life processes, whereas things that are used constitute the durable world built by homo faber that stands in contrast to mere life.

Animal laborans views nature as the provider of good things to be taken and consumed, while homo faber views nature as furnishing almost worthless materials whose value comes entirely from work performed upon them.
distinctions.item_a: nature seen through the eyes of the animal laborans
distinctions.item_b: nature seen through the eyes of homo faber

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between consumer society processes and the enduring world of use.
The dual necessity of consumption for survival and durability for human existence.
extraction.segment_function: conclusion

definitions.definition: The maker who literally works upon materials and fabricates the things that constitute the human artifice.
The laborer who labors and mixes with biological processes.

distinctions.distinction: Work is the activity of hands by homo faber that makes and works upon things to create a durable human artifice, whereas labor is the activity of animal laborans that mixes with biological processes.
Destruction is inherent in consumption, whereas wear is incidental to use, as use objects possess an independence and durability that allows them to survive even when unused.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between homo faber and animal laborans.
The role of durability and objectivity in stabilizing human life and identity.
extraction.segment_function: The block defines the distinction between work and labor through the concepts of homo faber, the human artifice, durability, and objectivity, contrasting the stability of man-made things with the cyclical nature of biological consumption.

claims.claim: Fabrication by homo faber involves reification, which inherently entails a violation and destruction of nature by removing materials from their natural locations.
qualifications: applies to fabrication and homo faber
claims.supporting_excerpt: Fabrication, the work of homo faber , consists in reification. Solidity, inherent in all, even the most fragile, things, comes from the material worked upon, but this material itself is not simply given and there, like the fruits of field and trees which we may gather or leave alone without changing the household of nature. Material is already a product of human hands which have removed it from its natural location, either killing a life process, as in the case of the tree which must be destroyed in order to provide wood, or interrupting one of nature’s slower processes, as in the case of iron, stone, or marble torn out of the womb of the earth. This element of violation and violence is present in all fabrication, and homo faber , the creator of the human artifice, has always been a destroyer of nature.

claims.claim: Human productivity modeled after a Creator-God necessarily results in a Promethean revolt because it builds a man-made world by destroying part of God-created nature.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Since his productivity was seen in the image of a Creator-God, so that where God creates ex nihilo , man creates out of given substance, human productivity was by definition bound to result in a Promethean revolt because it could erect a man-made world only after destroying part of God-created nature.

definitions.definition: The work of homo faber that consists in reification and involves the violation and destruction of nature.

distinctions.distinction: The animal laborans remains the servant of nature and the earth, whereas homo faber conducts himself as lord and master of the whole earth.

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between labor (tilled soil needing repeated labor) and true reification/fabrication.
The inherent violence and destruction of nature in human fabrication.
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: The actual work of fabrication is guided by a model that precedes the process and exists outside the fabricator.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The actual work of fabrication is performed under the guidance of a model in accordance with which the object is constructed. This model can be an image beheld by the eye of the mind or a blueprint in which the image has already found a tentative materialization through work. In either case, what guides the work of fabrication is outside the fabricator and precedes the actual work process

claims.claim: The process of making is entirely determined by the categories of means and end.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The process of making is itself entirely determined by the categories of means and end.

definitions.definition: Multiplies something that already possesses a relatively stable, relatively permanent existence in the world, distinct from mere repetition.

distinctions.distinction: Multiplication multiplies something possessing relatively permanent existence in the world, whereas repetition is urged upon and remains subject to the biological cycle of the human body.

extraction.segment_function: Examines the role of models, means-end categories, and the distinction between multiplication and repetition in the work of fabrication within the vita activa.

claims.claim: Fabrication is distinguished from all other human activities by having a definite beginning and a predictable end.
claims.supporting_excerpt: To have a definite beginning and a definite, predictable end is the mark of fabrication, which through this characteristic alone dis tinguishes itself from all other human activities.

claims.claim: Homo faber is a master of himself and his doings because he is alone with his image of the future product and free to produce or destroy.
qualifications: True neither of the animal laborans nor of the man of action
claims.supporting_excerpt: Homo faber is indeed a lord and master, not only because he is the master or has set himself up as the master of all nature but because he is master of himself and his doings.

definitions.definition: An activity marked by having a definite beginning and a predictable and not irreversible end, associated with homo faber.

distinctions.distinction: Fabrication has a definite and predictable beginning and end and is not irreversible, whereas labor is caught in the cyclical movement of the body's life process and has neither a beginning nor an end.

extraction.segment_function: The block analyzes the distinctions between fabrication (work), labor, and action, focusing on the role of instrumentality, tools, machines, and the loss of the means-end distinction when tools are absorbed into the cyclic rhythm of animal laborans.

claims.claim: Unlike tools which remain servants of the hand, machines demand that the laborer serve them by adjusting the natural rhythm of the body to mechanical movement.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Unlike the tools of workmanship, which at every given moment in the work process remain the servants of the hand, the machines demand that the laborer serve them, that he adjust the natural rhythm of his body to their mechanical movement.

claims.claim: The first stage of modern technology, marked by the steam engine and industrial revolution, was characterized by the imitation of natural processes and the use of natural forces, powered by newly discovered coal mines.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The first stage, the invention of the steam engine, which led into the industrial revolution, was still characterized by an imitation of natural processes and the use of natural forces for human purposes, which did not differ in principle from the old use of water and wind power.

distinctions.distinction: Tools remain the servants of the hand at every moment in the work process and cannot guide or replace the hand, whereas machines demand that the laborer serve them and adjust to their movement, eventually replacing the body's labor altogether.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between tools and machines regarding human adjustment and bodily rhythm.
The historical stages of modern technology: the steam engine/industrial revolution stage versus the electrical/continuous process stage.
extraction.segment_function: Analyze the distinction between tools and machines, and outline the stages of modern technology from the steam engine to electricity and continuous processes.

claims.claim: The channeling of natural forces into the human world has shattered the purposefulness of the world.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The channeling of natural forces into the human world has shattered the very purposefulness of the world, the fact that objects are the ends for which tools and implements are designed.

claims.claim: In automation, the distinction between operation and product, along with the product's precedence over operation, has become obsolete.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In the mode of production ushered in by automation, the distinction between operation and product, as well as the product’s precedence over the operation (which is only the means to produce the end), no longer make sense and have become obsolete.

definitions.definition: Things that are not made but grow by themselves into whatever they become, originating from the Latin nasci or the Greek physis.
Courses of movement which are self-moving and therefore outside the range of wilful and purposeful interference.

distinctions.distinction: A natural thing's existence is not separate but is identical with the process through which it comes into being, whereas the products of human hands must be realized step by step and their fabrication process is entirely distinct from the existence of the fabricated thing itself.

extraction.segment_function: The author analyzes automation as the culminating point of modern technology, explaining how the introduction of natural and cosmic processes into the human world shatters the purposefulness of the human artifice, overturns the categories of homo faber, and shifts the fundamental question of technology from human comfort to whether machines and automatic processes now rule over the human world.
unresolved_context: The potential of future technology to channel universal forces of the cosmos around us into the nature of the earth.

claims.claim: The continuous automatic process of manufacturing has replaced human standards of utility and beauty with machine-determined product shapes and biological life-process functions.
qualifications: In the context of the continuous automatic process of manufacturing
claims.supporting_excerpt: the continuous automatic process of manufacturing has not only done away with the “unwarranted assumption” that “human hands guided by human brains represent the optimum efficiency,” 15 but with the much more important assumption that the things of the world around us should depend upon human design and be built in accordance with human standards of either utility or beauty.

claims.claim: In the work and fabrication of homo faber, the end justifies the means and organizes the entire work process, but utilitarian ends are perpetually transformed into further means.
qualifications: Relates to homo faber and the activity of fabrication
claims.supporting_excerpt: The implements and tools of homo faber , from which the most fundamental experience of instrumentality arises, determine all work and fabrication. Here it is indeed true that the end justifies the means; it does more, it produces and organizes them.

definitions.definition: The maker and fabricator whose tools and implements determine the fundamental experience of instrumentality, work, and fabrication.

distinctions.distinction: Technology increasingly appears not as a conscious human effort for material power, but as a biological development transplanting innate human organism structures into the environment.
distinctions.item_b: conscious human effort to enlarge material power

extraction.segment_function: Analyzing how automatic manufacturing, machine production, and the activity of homo faber redefine instrumentality, replacing traditional human standards of utility and beauty with biological processes and endless chains of means and ends.

claims.claim: Consistent utilitarianism suffers from an innate incapacity to distinguish between utility and meaningfulness.
qualifications: Inherent in all consistent utilitarianism
claims.supporting_excerpt: This perplexity, inherent in all consistent utilitarianism, the philosophy of homo faber par excellence, can be diagnosed theoretically as an innate incapacity to understand the distinction between utility and meaningfulness

claims.claim: Establishing utility as meaning generates meaninglessness because it traps thought in an endless chain of means and ends.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The perplexity of utilitarianism is that it gets caught in the unending chain of means and ends without ever arriving at some principle which could justify the category of means and end, that is, of utility itself. The “in order to” has become the content of the “for the sake of”; in other words, utility established as meaning generates meaninglessness.

definitions.definition: The relational status of being a means 'in order to' achieve something else.
A domain expressed linguistically by 'for the sake of' that defies questioning about its own use.

distinctions.distinction: Utility is expressed as 'in order to,' whereas meaningfulness is expressed as 'for the sake of.'

must_not_be_lost: The inherent perplexity of utilitarianism involving the unending chain of means and ends.
The paradox that homo faber as pure fabricator cannot comprehend meaning except as a paradoxical end in itself.
extraction.segment_function: Analyzing the utilitarian perplexities of homo faber, the inability to distinguish utility from meaningfulness, and the resulting slide into meaninglessness.

claims.claim: Homo faber's instrumentalization involves degrading all things into means, leading to a loss of intrinsic and independent value for both manufactured objects and natural forces.
qualifications: In so far as man is homo faber
claims.supporting_excerpt: Man, in so far as he is homo faber , instrumentalizes, and his instrumentalization implies a degradation of all things into means, their loss of intrinsic and independent value, so that eventually not only the objects of fabrication but also “the earth in general and all forces of nature,” which clearly came into being without the help of man and have an existence independent of the human world, lose their “value

claims.claim: The generalization of the fabrication experience turns usefulness and utility into ultimate standards for life and the world, transforming every end into a means.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The issue at stake is, of course, not instrumentality, the use of means to achieve an end, as such, but rather the generalization of the fabrication experience in which usefulness and utility are established as the ultimate standards for life and the world of men.

definitions.definition: A term applied by classical Greeks to the arts and crafts, best translated by philistine, implying vulgarity of thinking and acting in terms of expediency.

distinctions.distinction: From the viewpoint of fabrication, the finished product is an end in itself; productive and limited instrumentality changes into limitless instrumentalization only when the life process takes hold of things and uses them for its purposes.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between limited instrumentality in fabrication and the limitless instrumentalization caused by the life process.
Plato's counter-argument to Protagoras regarding man as the measure of use things.
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: The modern age aimed to exclude political man (who acts and speaks) from its public realm, much as antiquity sought to exclude homo faber.
qualifications: In both instances the exclusion was not a matter of course
claims.supporting_excerpt: The truth of this remark lies in the fact that the modern age was as intent on excluding political man, that is, man who acts and speaks, from its public realm as antiquity was on excluding homo faber.

claims.claim: Homo faber forms a public realm of his own through the exchange market, driven by the need to show hand-made products and receive esteem.
qualifications: even though it may not be a political realm, properly speaking
claims.supporting_excerpt: His public realm is the exchange market, where he can show the products of his hand and receive the esteem which is due him.

definitions.definition: The builder of the world and producer of things whose products are produced in isolation.

distinctions.distinction: Animal laborans has a worldless, herdlike social life and cannot build a public worldly realm, whereas homo faber is fully capable of having a public realm of his own (the exchange market).

must_not_be_lost: The modern age based its view of society on the productivity of homo faber.
Isolation is a necessary condition for craftsmanship and mastership.
Conspicuous production is a trait of a society of producers.
extraction.segment_function: To analyze the public realm of homo faber (the exchange market), contrast modern exclusion of political man with ancient exclusions, and examine the necessity of isolation for craftsmanship.

claims.claim: Teamwork is destructive to workmanship because it relies on the division of labor and breaks down operations into constituent motions.
claims.supporting_excerpt: There can be hardly anything more alien or even more destructive to workmanship than teamwork, which actually is only a variety of the division of labor and presupposes the “breakdown of operations into their simple constituent motions.”

claims.claim: The exchange market served historically as the last public realm connected to the activity of homo faber.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Historically, the last public realm, the last meeting place which is at least connected with the activity of homo faber , is the exchange market on which his products are displayed.

definitions.definition: A variety of the division of labor that presupposes the breakdown of operations into simple constituent motions.

distinctions.distinction: Manufacturing society judges men as producers according to the quality of their products, whereas a laboring society judges men according to the functions they perform in the labor process.

extraction.segment_function: To analyze the relationship between workmanship, teamwork, commercial society, and the transition from homo faber to laboring society.

claims.claim: Value is exclusively acquired in the public realm through appearance and esteem, distinguishing it from the intrinsic natural worth possessed by a thing in privacy.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Value is the quality a thing can never possess in privacy but acquires automatically the moment it appears in public.

claims.claim: The inherent concept of value entails universal relativity and the loss of intrinsic worth, as things exist only in relation to other things and depend on the fluctuating estimations of supply and demand.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Universal relativity, that a thing exists only in relation to other things, and loss of intrinsic worth, that nothing any longer possesses an “objective” value independent of the ever-changing estimations of supply and demand, are inherent in the very concept of value itself.

definitions.definition: A quality a thing acquires automatically the moment it appears in public, consisting solely in the esteem of the public realm where things appear as commodities.
An objective quality of a thing itself, existing outside the will of the individual purchaser or seller, attached to the thing itself whether one likes it or not.

distinctions.distinction: Marketable value is altered by the alteration of a commodity's proportion to something else in the exchange market, whereas the intrinsic worth of a thing can be changed only through the actual physical change of the thing itself.

must_not_be_lost: Value comes into existence only in the exchange market and public realm.
Homo faber cannot bear the loss of absolute standards caused by universal relativity in exchange.
extraction.segment_function: To analyze the distinction between the intrinsic worth of things and their exchange value or marketable value within the public realm, and to trace how the rise of value as a relational concept undermines absolute standards.

claims.claim: Works of art possess supreme durability and distinct uselessness, standing apart from ordinary use objects and exchange markets.
qualifications: applies specifically to works of art within the human artifice
claims.supporting_excerpt: Among the things that give the human artifice the stability without which it could never be a reliable home for men are a number of objects which are strictly without any utility whatsoever and which, moreover, because they are unique, are not exchangeable and therefore defy equalization through a common denominator such as money

claims.claim: The immediate source of the art work is the human capacity for thought.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The immediate source of the art work is the human capacity for thought, as man’s “propensity to truck and barter” is the source of exchange objects, and as his ability to use is the source of use things.

definitions.definition: Objects that give the human artifice stability, are strictly without utility, are unique and non-exchangeable, and possess an outstanding permanence untouched by the corroding effect of natural processes.

distinctions.distinction: Proper intercourse with art requires removing it carefully from the whole context of ordinary use objects and daily wants, whereas ordinary use objects are subject to use that can destroy art.
distinctions.item_a: proper intercourse with a work of art

must_not_be_lost: Art objects achieve their permanence through uselessness and freedom from daily use.
Thought is the human capacity from which art works spring, transforming internal feelings into reified worldly things.
extraction.segment_function: To analyze the permanence of works of art as objects without utility that provide the human artifice with ultimate durability and represent worldly stability and a premonition of mortality's achievement.
unresolved_context: Plato's view on Protagoras and a god as the measure of all things.

claims.claim: Art works involve reification as transfiguration, a metamorphosis where thought becomes tangible reality through workmanship.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In the case of art works, reification is more than mere transformation; it is transfiguration, a veritable metamorphosis in which it is as though the course of nature which wills that all fire burn to ashes is reverted and even dust can burst into flames.

claims.claim: Thought and cognition are distinct, with cognition pursuing definite aims and ending when reached, whereas thought has no external end or aim.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Thought and cognition are not the same. Thought, the source of art works, is manifest without transformation or transfiguration in all great philosophy, whereas the chief manifestation of the cognitive processes, by which we acquire and store up knowledge, is the sciences. Cognition always pursues a definite aim, which can be set by practical considerations as well as by “idle curiosity”; but once this aim is reached, the cognitive process has come to an end. Thought, on the contrary, has neither an end nor an aim outside itself, and it does not even produce results

definitions.definition: The source of art works and great philosophy that has neither an end nor an aim outside itself and does not produce results.
The process by which we acquire and store up knowledge, pursuing a definite aim that concludes when the aim is reached.

distinctions.distinction: Cognition always pursues a definite aim and ends when reached, whereas thought has no end or aim outside itself and produces no results.

extraction.segment_function: To analyze the distinctions between reification and transfiguration in art, the nature of poetry and language, and the fundamental differences between thought and cognition.

claims.claim: Logical reasoning and intelligence resemble biological labor power and operate through compulsory brain processes akin to the physical laws of nature.
qualifications: applies to intelligence and logical reasoning rather than thought and cognition
claims.supporting_excerpt: In these human faculties we are actually confronted with a sort of brain power which in more than one respect resembles nothing so much as the labor power the human animal develops in its metabolism with nature.

claims.claim: Every manufactured thing transcends pure instrumentality and functional use through its shape, appearing publicly as either beautiful, ugly, or in-between.
qualifications: dependent on having a shape and appearing publicly
claims.supporting_excerpt: By the same token, namely, in its sheer worldly existence, every thing also transcends the sphere of pure instrumentality once it is completed.

definitions.definition: Mental processes that feed on brain power, producing logical operations that can be measured like bodily strength and governed by the laws of logic rooted in brain structure.

distinctions.distinction: Thought and cognition are distinct from the power of logical reasoning, which resembles biological labor power and operates via compulsive brain processes.

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between intelligence/logical reasoning and true thought/cognition.
The connection between a thing's shape, public appearance, and its transcendence of pure usefulness.
extraction.segment_function: Distinguish logical reasoning and intelligence from thought and cognition, compare intelligence to biological labor power, and analyze the relationship between utility, durability, shape, and beauty in worldly objects.

claims.claim: The man-made world of things becomes a durable home for mortal men only when it transcends both the functionalism of consumer goods and the sheer utility of objects produced for use.
qualifications: requires transcendence of sheer functionalism and utility to achieve stability
claims.supporting_excerpt: The man-made world of things, the human artifice erected by homo faber , becomes a home for mortal men, whose stability will endure and outlast the ever-changing movement of their lives and actions, only insomuch as it transcends both the sheer functionalism of things produced for consumption and the sheer utility of objects produced for use.

claims.claim: Acting and speaking men require the help of homo faber in his highest capacity, such as artists, poets, and writers, so that the stories they enact and tell can survive.
qualifications: relies on homo faber in his highest capacity
claims.supporting_excerpt: acting and speaking men need the help of homo faber in his highest capacity, that is, the help of the artist, of poets and historiographers, of monument-builders or writers, because without them the only product of their activity, the story they enact and tell, would not survive at all.

must_not_be_lost: The human artifice must be a place fit for action and speech to serve as a home for men on earth.
The measure of the human artifice can be neither biological necessity nor utilitarian instrumentalism.
extraction.segment_function: Conclude the analysis of the human artifice by explaining how the man-made world becomes a stable home for mortal men through transcending mere utility and by requiring the help of artists, poets, and writers to preserve the otherwise fleeting products of action and speech.

claims.claim: Human plurality has a twofold character of equality, which enables understanding and planning across generations, and distinction, which makes speech and action necessary for communication.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Human plurality, the basic condition of both action and speech, has the twofold character of equality and distinction.

claims.claim: Through speech and action, human beings reveal their unique distinctness and appear to each other as persons rather than merely as physical objects.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Speech and action reveal this unique distinctness. Through them, men distinguish themselves instead of being merely distinct; they are the modes in which human beings appear to each other, not indeed as physical objects, but qua men.

definitions.definition: The basic condition of action and speech possessing the twofold character of equality and distinction.
The curious quality of alteritas possessed by everything that is, transcending every particular quality.
To take an initiative, to begin, to set something into motion.

distinctions.distinction: Otherness is shared with everything that is and has its most abstract form in the multiplication of inorganic objects, whereas distinctness is shared with everything alive, and in man, distinctness and otherness combine into uniqueness.
The beginning introduced by action is not the beginning of the world or the beginning of something, but of somebody who is a beginner himself.
distinctions.item_b: The beginning introduced by human action

must_not_be_lost: Human plurality entails both equality and distinction.
Speech and action constitute the insertion of oneself into the human world as a second birth.
The principle of freedom and the principle of beginning came into the world with the creation of man.
extraction.segment_function: To define human plurality, distinctness, uniqueness, and the foundational role of speech and action in revealing the unique agent within the vita activa.

claims.claim: The revelatory quality of speech and action emerges in sheer human togetherness where people are neither for nor against each other.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This revelatory quality of speech and action comes to the fore where people are with others and neither for nor against them—that is, in sheer human togetherness.

claims.claim: When action loses the disclosure of the agent and becomes merely a means to an end, it ceases to transcend productive activity.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Without the disclosure of the agent in the act, action loses its specific character and becomes one form of achievement among others.

must_not_be_lost: Action needs the public realm and glory to fully disclose the agent together with the act.
Attempts to state who somebody is in words tend to describe what he is as a type or character, missing his specific uniqueness.
extraction.segment_function: The block analyzes the revelatory quality of speech and action in human togetherness, contrasting it with anonymity (good works and crime), discussing how action loses its unique character when reduced to means-ends achievement, and examining the intangibility and philosophic difficulty of expressing the unique 'who' of a person in language.

claims.claim: Human lives tell stories and history becomes the storybook of mankind because both are the outcome of action, resulting in stories with many actors and speakers yet without any tangible authors.
claims.supporting_excerpt: the reason why each human life tells its story and why history ultimately becomes the storybook of mankind, with many actors and speakers and yet without any tangible authors, is that both are the outcome of action.

claims.claim: Plato invented the metaphor of an actor behind the scenes pulling the strings because human affairs and the outcome of action lack a single author, leading him to view human affairs as lacking great seriousness.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Plato, who had no inkling of the modern concept of history, should have been the first to invent the metaphor of an actor behind the scenes who, behind the backs of acting men, pulls the strings and is responsible for the story.

distinctions.distinction: The fictional story was made up by an author who pulls the strings and directs the play, whereas the real story has no visible or invisible maker because it is not made at all.
Who somebody is can only be known by knowing the story of which he is the hero, whereas everything else known about him, including the work he produced, tells us only what he is or was.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between real stories without an author and fictional stories with a maker.
The role of action in producing history and human biographies.
extraction.segment_function: Analyzing why human affairs lack a tangible author and how philosophies of history and political philosophy invent the metaphor of an invisible maker.

claims.claim: Greek and Latin languages contain two interrelated words for the verb 'to act', reflecting an original division between the initial beginning made by a single person and the subsequent achievement carried out by many.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In order to illustrate what is at stake here we may remember that Greek and Latin, unlike the modern languages, contain two altogether different and yet interrelated words with which to designate the verb “to act.”

claims.claim: Action inherently possesses a boundless quality because every reaction acts as a new independent action that triggers chain reactions, meaning even the smallest act in limited circumstances can change every constellation.
qualifications: applies regardless of the specific content of action
claims.supporting_excerpt: These consequences are boundless, because action, though it may proceed from nowhere, so to speak, acts into a medium where every reaction becomes a chain reaction and where every process is the cause of new processes.

definitions.definition: An activity performed among and in relation to other acting beings where the actor is simultaneously a doer and a sufferer, characterized by boundless consequences, chain reactions, and the establishment of relationships.

distinctions.distinction: The former originally designated the beginning, leading, or setting into motion of an enterprise by a single person, whereas the latter originally designated the achievement, bearing, and finishing of the enterprise in which many join.

must_not_be_lost: The historical shift from primus inter pares leadership to isolated ruler-subject dynamics.
The connection between the human condition of natality and the inherent frailty of human institutions and laws.
Moderation as a primary political virtue and hubris as the political temptation par excellence.
extraction.segment_function: Analyzing the Greek and Latin etymology of action, the historical shift from interdependence to ruler-subject relations, and the inherent boundlessness, unpredictability, and relationship-establishing capacity of human action that makes human affairs frail.

claims.claim: The ancient Greek concept of action was highly individualistic, stressing self-disclosure and serving as the prototype of action and the agonal spirit in city-states.
claims.supporting_excerpt: No doubt this concept of action is highly individualistic, as we would say today. 20 It stresses the urge toward self-disclosure at the expense of all other factors and therefore remains relatively untouched by the predicament of unpredictability. As such it became the prototype of action for Greek antiquity and influenced, in the form of the so-called agonal spirit, the passionate drive to show one’s self in measuring up against others that underlies the concept of politics prevalent in the city-states.
