claims.claim: Greeks treated legislation and city-building as prepolitical activities of making (poiēsis) rather than action (praxis), comparing lawmakers to builders and craftsmen.
claims.supporting_excerpt: An outstanding symptom of this prevailing influence is that the Greeks, in distinction from all later developments, did not count legislating among the political activities. In their opinion, the lawmaker was like the builder of the city wall, someone who had to do and finish his work before political activity could begin.

distinctions.distinction: Action involves non-tangible, utterly fragile, boundlessly uncertain meaning, whereas making produces a tangible product with a clearly recognizable end and greater reliability.

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between Greek view of legislation as prepolitical making versus Roman or modern views.
The characterization of action as self-disclosure and the agonal spirit.
extraction.segment_function: Examine the Greek concept of action as individualistic self-disclosure, the agonal spirit, the prepolitical status of legislation and city-building as making (poiēsis), and the Socratic school's preference for making over the uncertainty of action (praxis).

claims.claim: Power is generated and kept alive solely by the living together of people in action and organization, and whoever isolates himself forfeits power.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The only indispensable material factor in the generation of power is the living together of people. Only where men live so close together that the potentialities of action are always present can power remain with them, and the foundation of cities, which as city-states have remained paradigmatic for all Western political organization, is therefore indeed the most important material prerequisite for power.

claims.claim: Tyranny rests fundamentally on isolation and contradicts human plurality, thereby generating impotence rather than power.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Montesquieu realized that the outstanding characteristic of tyranny was that it rested on isolation—on the isolation of the tyrant from his subjects and the isolation of the subjects from each other through mutual fear and suspicion—and hence that tyranny was not one form of government among others but contradicted the essential human condition of plurality

definitions.definition: The potentiality in being together, kept alive through organization and remaining together, corresponding to human plurality and boundless in nature.
An individual physical attribute that is indivisible, kept in bounds by plurality, and distinct from the power of collective action.
That which one man alone can exert against fellow men, associated with violence and the means of violence, which can destroy power but never substitute for it.

distinctions.distinction: Power depends on the agreement of many wills in being together and is boundless and divisible, whereas strength is an individual physical characteristic that is indivisible and bounded by the presence of others.
Power is generated by people living together in plurality, whereas force can be exerted by a single individual or few through violence and can destroy power but never substitute for it.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between power, strength, and force.
Montesquieu's insight that tyranny rests on isolation and contradicts human plurality.
extraction.segment_function: Analyzing the nature of power, strength, force, and their relationship to human plurality, organization, and tyranny.

claims.claim: The calamities of action arise from human plurality, which is essential for the public realm, making attempts to abolish plurality equivalent to abolishing the public realm.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The calamities of action all arise from the human condition of plurality, which is the condition sine qua non for that space of appearance which is the public realm. Hence the attempt to do away with this plurality is always tantamount to the abolition of the public realm itself.

claims.claim: Political philosophy since Plato can be interpreted as various attempts to escape politics through the concept of rule, which rests on a suspicion of action and a desire to find a substitute for it.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Escape from the frailty of human affairs into the solidity of quiet and order has in fact so much to recommend it that the greater part of political philosophy since Plato could easily be interpreted as various attempts to find theoretical foundations and practical ways for an escape from politics altogether.

definitions.definition: The human condition that is the condition sine qua non for the space of appearance which constitutes the public realm.
The notion that men can lawfully and politically live together only when some are entitled to command and the others forced to obey.

distinctions.distinction: Plato opened a gulf between these two modes of action, which were traditionally interconnected, separating the beginner who rules from those who execute orders.

must_not_be_lost: Plato's introduction of the division between those who know and do not act and those who act and do not know.
extraction.segment_function: The author analyzes how traditional political philosophy attempts to escape the frailty and dangers of human plurality and action through the establishment of one-man rule and the concept of rule itself, tracing this substitution primarily to Plato's separation of beginning and achieving.

claims.claim: The natural sciences have become exclusively sciences of process because the underlying human capacity that brought about this development is the human ability to act and start new unprecedented processes.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The very fact that natural sciences have become exclusively sciences of process and, in their last stage, sciences of potentially irreversible, irremediable “processes of no return” is a clear indication that, whatever the brain power necessary to start them, the actual underlying human capacity which alone could bring about this development is no “theoretical” capacity, neither contemplation nor reason, but the human ability to act—to start new unprecedented processes whose outcome remains uncertain and unpre dictable whether they are let loose in the human or the natural realm.

claims.claim: Men have never been and never will be able to undo or reliably control any of the processes they start through action.
claims.supporting_excerpt: men never have been and never will be able to undo or even to control reliably any of the processes they start through action.

must_not_be_lost: The central concept of modern natural and historical sciences is the concept of process, grounded in the human capacity for action.
extraction.segment_function: Analyze the process character of action in modern natural and historical sciences, highlighting the capacity to start irreversible processes and the resulting unpredictability and inability to undo deeds.

claims.claim: The moral codes inferred from the faculties of forgiving and making promises are entirely based on the presence of others rather than self-relation.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The moral code, on the other hand, inferred from the faculties of forgiving and of making promises, rests on experiences which nobody could ever have with himself, which, on the contrary, are entirely based on the presence of others.

claims.claim: Jesus of Nazareth discovered the role of forgiveness in the realm of human affairs, which holds a strictly secular significance independent of its religious articulation.
qualifications: Articulated in a religious context and language
claims.supporting_excerpt: The discoverer of the role of forgiveness in the realm of human affairs was Jesus of Nazareth. The fact that he made this discovery in a religious context and articulated it in religious language is no reason to take it any less seriously in a strictly secular sense.

definitions.definition: A form of rule whose legitimacy rests upon the domination of the self and whose guiding principles are established between me and myself.

distinctions.distinction: Platonic rulership draws guiding principles from a relationship established between me and myself, whereas the moral code of forgiving and promising rests on experiences entirely based on the presence of others.
distinctions.item_b: Moral code of forgiving and making promises

must_not_be_lost: Forgiving and promising correspond to the human condition of plurality and establish guiding principles distinct from Platonic self-rule.
Jesus of Nazareth is identified as the discoverer of forgiveness in human affairs, functioning as a necessary corrective for everyday trespassing and allowing men to remain free agents.
extraction.segment_function: To analyze the faculties of forgiving and promising as moral codes grounded in human plurality, contrasting Platonic rulership with Jesus of Nazareth's discovery of forgiveness as an essential corrective within human affairs.

claims.claim: The force that keeps people together in public space is mutual promise or contract, which generates a limited reality of sovereignty.
qualifications: applies when many are mutually bound by promises
sovereignty assumes a limited reality
claims.supporting_excerpt: The force that keeps them together, as distinguished from the space of appearances in which they gather and the power which keeps this public space in existence, is the force of mutual promise or contract. Sovereignty, which is always spurious if claimed by an isolated single entity, be it the individual entity of the person or the collective entity of a nation, assumes, in the case of many men mutually bound by promises, a certain limited reality.

claims.claim: Action is the one miracle-working faculty of man that interrupts the automatic, inexorable course of daily life and historical fatality.
qualifications: seen from the viewpoint of automatic processes
claims.supporting_excerpt: Action is, in fact, the one miracle-working faculty of man

distinctions.distinction: sovereignty can only be achieved by the many bound together, whereas mastership is conceivable only in isolation.
distinctions.item_a: sovereignty in the realm of action and human affairs
distinctions.item_b: mastership in the realm of making and the world of things

must_not_be_lost: The faculty of promising and forgiving as control mechanisms born directly out of living together.
Natality as the condition that men are born in order to begin rather than just to die.
extraction.segment_function: conclusion

claims.claim: Three foundational events determine the character of the modern age: the discovery of America and exploration of the earth, the Reformation and its resulting expropriation and accumulation of social wealth, and the invention of the telescope along with a new universal science.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Three great events stand at the threshold of the modern age and determine its character: the discovery of America and the ensuing exploration of the whole earth; the Reformation, which by expropriating ecclesiastical and monastic possessions started the twofold process of individual expropriation and the accumulation of social wealth; the invention of the telescope and the development of a new science that considers the nature of the earth from the viewpoint of the universe.

claims.claim: Speed has conquered space and rendered distance meaningless by eliminating the necessary time required to reach any point on earth.
qualifications: finds its limit at the unconquerable boundary of the simultaneous presence of one body at two different places
claims.supporting_excerpt: Speed has conquered space; and though this conquering process finds its limit at the unconquerable boundary of the simultaneous presence of one body at two different places, it has made distance meaningless, for no significant part of a human life—years, months, or even weeks—is any longer necessary to reach any point on the earth.

must_not_be_lost: The three foundational events marking the threshold of the modern age.
The relationship between the shrinkage of the globe and the conquest of space by speed.
extraction.segment_function: Introduction of the chapter on the modern age, identifying the three foundational events that threshold the modern era and discussing the historical trajectory of world alienation and earth shrinkage.
unresolved_context: Franz Kafka quote regarding the Archimedean point and its conditions.

claims.claim: Galileo's use of the telescope marked an unprecedented event that delivered the secrets of the universe to human cognition with the certainty of sense-perception.
claims.supporting_excerpt: What Galileo did and what nobody had done before was to use the telescope in such a way that the secrets of the universe were delivered to human cognition “with the certainty of sense-perception”

claims.claim: Prior speculations and philosophical hypotheses, such as those of Copernicus and Bruno, lacked the status of an objective historical event until confirmed by empirical facts delivered by the telescope.
qualifications: In the realm of ideas there are only originality and depth, but no absolute, objective novelty
claims.supporting_excerpt: However, neither the speculations of philosophers nor the imaginings of astronomers has ever constituted an event. Prior to the telescopic discoveries of Galileo, Giordano Bruno’s philosophy attracted little attention even among learned men, and without the factual confirmation they bestowed upon the Copernican revolution

distinctions.distinction: Ideas possess permanence and immortality based on inherent power of illumination independently of time and history, whereas historical events involve objective, factual novelty such as Galileo's telescopic discoveries.

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between speculative ideas of astronomers/philosophers and factual confirmation brought by Galileo's telescope.
The characterization of Galileo's intervention as bringing secrets of the universe within grasp of earth-bound senses with certainty.
extraction.segment_function: To analyze the historical and epistemological significance of Galileo's telescope and the scientific discoveries that initiated the modern age and earth alienation.

claims.claim: Modern philosophy began with Descartes' universal doubt, which replaced the ancient Greek thaumazein (wonder at everything that is) as the central position and motor of thought.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Modern philosophy began with Descartes’ de omnibus dubitandum est , with doubt, but with doubt not as an inherent control of the human mind to guard against deceptions of thought and illusions of sense, not as skepticism against the morals and prejudices of men and times, not even as a critical method in scientific inquiry and philosophic speculation. Cartesian doubt is much more far-reaching in scope and too fundamental in intent to be determined by such concrete contents. In modern philosophy and thought, doubt occupies much the same central position as that occupied for all the centuries before by the Greek thaumazein , the wonder at everything that is as it is.

definitions.definition: A radical and universal doubt occupying the central position in modern thought that doubts the existence of truth itself, resting on the premise that truth and reality do not simply appear of their own accord to human senses or reason.

distinctions.distinction: Ancient philosophy was the articulation of wonder (thaumazein), whereas modern philosophy consists in the articulations and ramifications of doubting.
distinctions.item_a: Ancient philosophy (from Plato and Aristotle to the modern age)

extraction.segment_function: Examines the historical rise of Cartesian doubt as the foundational principle of modern philosophy, contrasting it with ancient wonder and traditional assumptions about truth and appearance.
unresolved_context: The full implications of Kierkegaard's leap into belief from doubt in modern religion.
The exact mechanism by which the reading of an instrument defeated both mind and senses.

claims.claim: The most momentous and unavoidable spiritual consequence of modern discoveries has been the reversal of the hierarchical order between the vita contemplativa and the vita activa.
qualifications: follows closely upon the discovery of the Archimedean point and the concomitant rise of Cartesian doubt
claims.supporting_excerpt: Perhaps the most momentous of the spiritual consequences of the discoveries of the modern age and, at the same time, the only one that could not have been avoided, since it followed closely upon the discovery of the Archimedean point and the concomitant rise of Cartesian doubt, has been the reversal of the hierarchical order between the vita contemplativa and the vita activa.

claims.claim: Modern technology originated exclusively in a non-practical search for useless knowledge rather than a pragmatic desire to improve earthly conditions or ease labor.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is a matter of historical record that modern technology has its origins not in the evolution of those tools man had always devised for the twofold purpose of easing his labors and erecting the human artifice, but exclusively in an altogether non-practical search for useless knowledge.

must_not_be_lost: Reversal of the hierarchical order between vita contemplativa and vita activa
Modern technology originating from non-practical search for useless knowledge rather than practical instincts

claims.claim: Homo faber was deprived of permanent measures preceding and outlasting the fabrication process due to the great revolution of modernity.
qualifications: arose from the great revolution of modernity
acquired undreamed-of ingenuity in devising instruments
claims.supporting_excerpt: Homo faber , in other words, as he arose from the great revolution of modernity, though he was to acquire an undreamed-of ingenuity in devising instruments to measure the infinitely large and the infinitely small, was deprived of those permanent measures that precede and outlast the fabrication process and form an authentic and reliable absolute with respect to the fabricating activity.

claims.claim: The principle of utility was superseded by the greatest happiness of the greatest number, reflecting the ultimate failure of homo faber to assert himself.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Nothing perhaps indicates clearer the ultimate failure of homo faber to assert himself than the rapidity with which the principle of utility, the very quintessence of his world view, was found wanting and was superseded by the principle of “the greatest happiness of the greatest number.”

definitions.definition: The sum total of pleasures minus pains, residing entirely on introspection as an inner sense.

distinctions.distinction: Pleasure enjoys something besides itself, whereas pain is completely independent of any object and makes one sense only oneself.

must_not_be_lost: The transition from homo faber and utility to animal laborans and the pain-and-pleasure calculus.
extraction.segment_function: Discussing the defeat of homo faber through the rise of utility, the principle of process, and the ultimate victory of animal laborans driven by pain, pleasure, and the pain and pleasure calculus.

claims.claim: Augustine distinguishes between the question 'Who am I?', directed by man at himself, and 'What am I?', addressed to God.
claims.supporting_excerpt: He distinguishes between the questions of “Who am I?” and “What am I?” the first being directed by man at himself (“And I directed myself at myself and said to me: You, who are you? And I answered: A man”— tu, quis es? [ Confessiones x. 6]) and the second being addressed to God (“What then am I, my God? What is my nature?”— Quid ergo sum, Deus meus? Quae natura sum? [x. 17]).

claims.claim: William L. Westermann argues that Aristotle's statement regarding craftsmen living in limited slavery implies that temporary work contracts forfeit specific elements of free status by volition.
qualifications: Citing William L. Westermann's historical interpretation
claims.supporting_excerpt: William L. Westermann (“Between Slavery and Freedom,” American Historical Review , Vol. L [1945]) holds that the “statement of Aristotle . . . that craftsmen live in a condition of limited slavery meant that the artisan, when he made a work contract, disposed of two of the four elements of his free status [viz., of freedom of economic activity and right of unrestricted movement], but by his own volition and for a temporary period”
